#9631. How CAD Software Thinks: B-rep, CSG, NURBS, and Their Role in AI-Generated Designs

Mechanical Engineering student at Carnegie Mellon University | Exploring engineering, technology, design, and innovation.

Mechanical Engineering student at Carnegie Mellon University | Exploring engineering, technology, design, and innovation.

Mechanical Engineering student at Carnegie Mellon University | Exploring engineering, technology, design, and innovation.

In my previous article, I laid out a test plan for checking whether large language models (LLMs) can write usable, manufacturable parametric parts. The idea I kept coming back to was that “it ran” is not the same as “it is correct.” But to understand how a script can run and still produce a bad part, or fail on a perfectly reasonable request, you need to know what the CAD software is doing underneath the script.

So, this article is the background chapter, written to stand on its own. It is for mechanical engineering students who use CAD every day but have never looked at how the software stores a shape, and for programmers who are curious about where AI and CAD meet.

A note on scope: I am a student, not a kernel developer. I have simplified some things, and where my understanding is limited, I say so and point to the books.

What you see on screen is a rendering. What the software stores is a definition from which the rendering, the volume, the mass properties, and the toolpaths can all be computed. Two ideas run through every representation:

File formats show the difference clearly. A STEP file (ISO 10303) can carry exact faces and edges, which is why you can open a STEP part in another CAD system and still select a face to modify it. An STL file carries only a list of triangles. That is enough for a slicer, but the exact cylinder of a drilled hole is gone, replaced by flat facets. STL also stores no units, so the software reading it has to assume them.

Most mechanical CAD systems describe a solid by its boundary. A B-rep has two layers. The topological layer holds faces, edges, and vertices and records how they are connected. The geometric layer attaches a surface to each face, a curve to each edge, and a point to each vertex. A drilled hole, for example, is a face lying on a cylindrical surface, bounded by two circular edges.

Even a plain box shows the structure: 6 faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices. For simple solids like this, Euler’s formula holds: V − E + F = 2, and 8 − 12 + 6 = 2. Martti Mäntylä’s book builds solid modeling around operators that preserve this kind of consistency, known as Euler operators. Solids with through-holes or faces with inner boundaries need extra terms in the formula.

Most kernels keep common shapes (planes, cylinders, cones, spheres, and tori) as exact analytic surfaces and use NURBS for freeform ones (Section 4). Commercial kernels such as Parasolid and ACIS, and the open-source OpenCASCADE kernel that CadQuery is built on, are all B-rep kernels.

The strength of B-rep is that features have handles: you can select a face and shell it, or select an edge and fillet it. The cost is complexity. A B-rep can be invalid: faces that do not quite meet, surfaces that intersect themselves, or inconsistent orientation. A viewer may display such a model without complaint while the kernel refuses to operate on it. This is why my test plan includes a validity check and does not stop at “it exports.”

For further reading: Aristides Requicha’s 1980 survey of rigid-solid representations is the classic overview, Christoph Hoffmann’s Geometric and Solid Modeling is a readable textbook, and Ian Stroud’s Boundary Representation Modelling Techniques focuses on how B-rep systems work in practice.

In CSG a shape is a tree. The leaves are primitives such as boxes, cylinders, and spheres, and the nodes are Boolean operations (union, difference, intersection) and transformations such as translate and rotate. A bracket with a hole is “a box minus a cylinder.” Requicha’s survey treats CSG as one of the main families of solid representation, and OpenSCAD is the best-known scripting tool built around it.

CSG is compact and natural to write as code, and a CSG model is mathematically well defined as long as its primitives are. The cost is that the tree describes how to build the shape, not what the finished faces and edges are. There is no direct way to say “round this edge,” because edges only exist after the tree is evaluated. In CSG tools, rounding edges usually needs workarounds.

A mesh approximates the surface with triangles. It stores vertex positions and which triangles they form, and nothing about design features, exact curves, or units. It is the standard hand-off format for 3D printing slicers, and for that purpose it works well. For engineering work, such as adding a tolerance or drilling a hole in the right place on an imported part, it is a poor starting point because the exact definition has been thrown away. Its accuracy depends on how finely the surface was triangulated.

Faces, edges, vertices, plus surfaces and curves

Tree of primitives and Boolean operations

NURBS stands for Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines. The standard reference is Les Piegl and Wayne Tiller’s The NURBS Book. A NURBS curve is defined by four ingredients:

The rational part, the weights, matters because ordinary polynomial splines cannot represent a circle exactly, while rational ones can. Piegl and Tiller show a full circle built from rational quadratic segments. This is one reason NURBS became the common language for CAD curves: one representation covers circles, ellipses, and sculpted freeform curves.

A NURBS surface extends the idea to a grid of control points with a knot vector in each direction. In a B-rep, a face is often a NURBS surface patch that is trimmed by the boundary curves of its edges. Gerald Farin’s Curves and Surfaces for CAGD and Michael Mortenson’s Geometric Modeling give broader introductions to the same mathematics.

My understanding is that this is one reason operations like fillets, shells, and offsets are harder than extrusions. The kernel has to compute new surfaces, such as a blend between two faces or a copy of a face pushed inward by the wall thickness. The exact offset of a freeform surface is generally not another NURBS surface of the same simple form, so it has to be approximated, trimmed, and stitched back into a watertight solid. A tiny gap or overlap, and the result is invalid.

Parametric CAD builds a part as a sequence: sketch a profile, extrude it, cut a hole, fillet an edge. Each step is an operation the kernel applies to the B-rep left by the previous step, and “parametric” means the sequence can be replayed with new values. Order matters. Filleting before cutting holes leaves different edges to work with than filleting after.

The hard part is referring to things. “Fillet this edge” requires a way to identify the edge. In interactive CAD, you click on it, and the software must remember which edge you meant when a parameter changes and the history is replayed. When the topology changes, such references can break or jump to the wrong entity. This is known as the topological naming problem, and it is widely discussed in the CAD community.

Code-based CAD avoids stored references by describing what to select with a rule. Here is a short CadQuery example:

The rule "|Z" means “edges parallel to Z.” A rule like this is robust when your intent is clear, but it can also match more or fewer edges than you meant, and a script that selects the wrong edges may still run. That is exactly the kind of gap between “it ran” and “it is correct” that I want to measure.

An LLM writes text. It never sees the B-rep. It writes a sequence of operations and, on a first attempt, has to predict what shape that sequence will produce: which way a sketch plane faces, which edges a selector will pick, whether a fillet radius will fit. The kernel is the one that finds out, and the model learns about it only if someone feeds the error message back, which is what the repair condition in my test plan does.

Researchers and users approach this in different ways:

Based on how the kernel works, here is where I expect problems to show up. These are reasoned risks, not test results:

Likely trouble spot for an AI-written part

A feature on the wrong plane or the wrong side of the part

A rule that picks more, fewer, or different edges than intended

Fillet before holes, or shell before cuts: valid but different (or invalid) geometry

NURBS-based operations (fillet, shell, offset)

The kernel works with plain numbers, so millimetres are only a convention and units can drift

You do not need to trust the script or distrust it. You need to check it. Here is the list I would use:

Knowing how a CAD kernel represents a shape tells you what to check when something else generates that shape. A solid is a boundary of faces and edges backed by exact surfaces, usually NURBS for the freeform ones. A script is a list of instructions the kernel has to carry out, and every instruction can fail in a way the script’s author cannot see. That is why “it ran” never settles the question.

The results of the test plan from my previous article will come in a separate article, once I have run the tests and can report real numbers instead of guesses.

Can AI Write CAD? Testing LLM-Generated 3D Models for Manufacturability

#9629. How to choose SLIs: a practical method, from DQL queries to objectives

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at span.observer

A team creates twenty SLOs in one afternoon, one per available metric. Three months later nobody looks at them: they are all green while users complain. The problem is not the tool, it is knowing how to choose SLIs.

Goal of this tutorial: apply a five-step method to choose SLIs from the user journey, write them in DQL, measure their history and derive realistic objectives. The queries target Dynatrace SaaS (Grail); the approach also applies to Dynatrace Managed, with metric expressions instead of DQL.

For the general SRE context, see AI and reliability: what SREs need to know.

CPU, memory or pod count remain useful for diagnosis. They are not SLIs.

Ask: « If this action fails, who calls support? » Keep three to five journeys at most. Example for an online shop:

For search: latency. For the basket: availability. For payment: availability and latency.

This is the step most often rushed. Write it down:

This definition decides what consumes the error budget. Have it validated by the product team.

Availability per day over 14 days, from spans:

Latency distribution, to choose the threshold:

Critical lines: filterOut removes health checks from the denominator. The url.path field depends on your instrumentation; adapt it. If your services are instrumented by OneAgent, the dt.service.request.count metric and its counterpart dt.service.request.failure_count give the same result faster (names to check in the Dynatrace documentation). Over 14 days, a query on spans can be costly: run it once, not in a loop.

On Managed, open Data Explorer with builtin:service.errors.server.rate and builtin:service.response.time (percentiles), split by day.

Simple rule: start from what the service already does, slightly below, then tighten if users demand it.

A 100% objective forbids any change. An objective above current performance is in permanent alert. Both are useless.

A Kubernetes node can fail without any user noticing, thanks to replicas. Conversely, a saturated database can slow down every payment while all pods are « healthy ». So keep infrastructure signals in your dashboards and diagnostic alerts, and reserve SLIs for user-facing signals. This separation reduces on-call noise and makes the error budget credible to product.

Creating the SLOs themselves is covered in creating an OpenTelemetry SLO in DQL.

No. Group the endpoints of the same journey. Only isolate a critical endpoint whose behaviour differs strongly (payment, for example).

The « requests under the threshold » ratio accumulates cleanly over a window and gives an error budget. The percentile remains useful to choose the threshold, in step 4.

Start with a cautious objective, mark it « provisional » and revise it after two weeks of data.

Choosing SLIs means starting from the user, defining good events precisely, measuring the history, then setting an achievable objective. An afternoon of method beats twenty SLOs that nobody reads.

Recommended next step: book the hour with your product owner this week, list the three most critical journeys, and run the step 4 queries on them. You will have defensible SLIs and objectives before the next planning session.

Keep each SLI definition, its query and its review date in the same place, so that the next person on call understands what the number means without asking.

#9628. The Simple Drink Swap Linked To 41% More Weight Loss

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

The water group also showed greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

Dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, said:

“It’s a small change with the potential for a big impact on long-term health outcomes.”

The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

#9626. How to Delete One Record From a Parquet Table Without Rewriting Everything

Software Engineer 20+ experience in data space - Data warehousing, Business Intelligence, Cloud Computing in data engineering space and AI

Software Engineer 20+ experience in data space - Data warehousing, Business Intelligence, Cloud Computing in data engineering space and AI

Software Engineer 20+ experience in data space - Data warehousing, Business Intelligence, Cloud Computing in data engineering space and AI

A while back I wrote about a service that handles deletion requests for a large data lake, and how we kept a MySQL table from falling over under the weight of its own status updates. I left one thread deliberately unplugged at the end of that piece: how do you actually delete a record from a Hive table when the underlying files are plain Parquet or JSON, formats with no Delete DML to lean on? That's the question I want to answer here.

This isn't specific to Hive or Parquet. It applies to any storage format that doesn't support row-level DELETE natively, whatever that format happens to be in your environment. Parquet on Hive is simply the concrete case I'm going to walk through, because it's the one we actually run, and it's still extremely common. Delta and Iceberg solve this problem at the table-format level for anyone already on them, but most data lakes that have grown organically over years are sitting on something older: plain Parquet or JSON files in S3, organized into Hive partitions, with no transaction log and no built-in concept of deleting a row. A file is a file. If a record in it needs to go, something has to produce a new file without that record and make it take the old one's place.

The naive version of this is to rewrite the whole partition, or worse, the whole table, every time a deletion needs to happen. That works, technically, but it means touching enormous amounts of data you never needed to touch just to remove a handful of rows, and doing it on a timeline that doesn't scale as the volume of deletion requests grows. The real problem isn't deleting a row. It's deleting a row without turning every request into a full-table rewrite.

It's worth being upfront about where this sits relative to Delta and Iceberg, since that's the first thing anyone on those formats will ask. InMobi's engineering team wrote a good piece on this which covers the same underlying problem on plain Parquet, and lands on the same conclusion most writing on this topic does: move to a format with native delete support. That's sound advice, and if you're starting fresh or dealing with a handful of tables, it's probably the right call.

It stops being the right call, the moment "move to Delta" means migrating thousands of tables owned by dozens of different teams across a large organization. That's not a setting you flip, it's a coordination problem: every team has to schedule the work, validate that downstream consumers still function against the new format, and prioritize it against everything else on their roadmap.

For a data lake with tens of thousands of existing assets, that migration is realistically a multi-year effort, and deletion requests don't pause for multi-year efforts. What follows is what we built for the tables that are in neither format today, and have no realistic path to being migrated any time soon.

There's also a second, more technical reason the deletion-vector approach isn't a full substitute even once you are migrated: a deletion vector only marks a row as deleted, the physical bytes stay in the old file until a separate compaction step runs later, which means the data isn't actually gone the moment the deletion request completes. For a regulatory deletion obligation, that gap matters on its own, independent of the migration question.

Before a table can have anything deleted from it, the team that owns it has to onboard it, and onboarding means answering two questions.

First, which column in this table maps to an index we can search by? A request comes in as something like a customer ID, and the table might store that same value under a completely different column name, customer_account_id instead of customerId, say. Every onboarded table declares that mapping up front, against a known list of valid index types we support.

Second, is the table append-only? Some tables are classic mutable datasets where existing rows can be updated or removed. Others are immutable by design, think hourly partitions of streamed event data that are written once and never touched again after that. This distinction matters enormously for how we go about finding what to delete, which is the next problem.

Parquet has no index. There's no structure telling you "the row with customerId X lives in file Y." For a mutable table, we still have to scan, there's no way around that, but we scan smart: using input_file_name(), we identify exactly which physical files within the table actually contain a matching record, rather than assuming we need to touch every file in every partition.

Immutable tables get a different treatment, because scanning the same ever-growing pile of historical partitions every single week doesn't hold up over time. For these, we run a pre-processing step we call indexing: a separate, lightweight table that just maps index_column_value to partition. Instead of scanning the whole table on every deletion cycle, we check this small index table first, get back a short list of partitions that actually matter, and only look there.

The indexing job runs as a pre-step before every deletion cycle, so it's always catching the new partitions that have accumulated since the last run. The index stays current without ever needing a full historical re-scan.

Once we know which files contain matching records, the deletion itself is narrow by design. For each affected file, we read it, filter out the rows that need to go, and write the result as a new file, abcd.parquet produces abcd_filtered.parquet. Once that filtered file is fully written, it takes over the original file's name and location, overwriting the S3 object the table actually reads from.

This is the part that makes the whole scheme safe to run without taking the table offline. An S3 object write is atomic. A reader querying the table mid-operation either sees the complete original file or the complete replacement, never anything in between. There's no partition-level lock, no window where a dashboard or another job sees a half-written or missing file. Other jobs and queries keep reading the table normally for the entire duration of the deletion run, because from their point of view, nothing is happening until the moment a file's contents change atomically underneath them.

For tables with a lot of partitions, we also parallelize the work itself. If a table has 220 partitions needing attention, we don't process them one at a time. We split the partition list into batches of fifty and run up to five parallel processes against them, four handling fifty partitions each and one picking up the remaining twenty. The targeted, file-level nature of the deletion is what makes this kind of parallel split straightforward: each batch only ever touches its own set of files, so there's no coordination needed between the parallel workers.

A deletion job that touches hundreds of partitions across parallel workers is going to fail partway through sometimes, a worker crashes, a cluster gets preempted, whatever the reason. The failure mode here is about as gentle as it gets: since the original file is never touched until the filtered replacement is completely written and ready to swap in, a crash before that point leaves the original table exactly as it was. Nothing is lost, nothing is corrupted, nothing is half-deleted.

The one cleanup responsibility we do take seriously is the staging area. Every table or partition split being processed gets its own staging location for the filtered files it's producing, and a finally block guarantees that location gets cleaned up whether the run succeeds or fails. Without that, a crashed run would leave orphaned _filtered files sitting around in S3 indefinitely, harmless to the table itself, but a quiet, creeping mess that nobody notices until someone goes looking for why a staging bucket is larger than it should be.

None of this complexity exists for its own sake. The alternative, rewriting entire partitions or whole tables on every deletion request, works at a small scale and becomes untenable at a large one. The targeted, file-level approach keeps the amount of data touched proportional to the amount of data actually changing, not to the size of the table it lives in. The indexing step for immutable tables exists for the same reason: avoiding a full historical scan every week is the difference between a deletion cycle that stays fast as the table grows, and one that gets slower every single week, forever.

The atomic swap and the finally-block cleanup are what let this run unattended, at scale, without anyone needing to watch it. Readers never see a bad state. A crash never corrupts anything. Those two guarantees are what actually make it possible to trust this as infrastructure other teams' compliance obligations depend on, not just a script that happens to work when nothing goes wrong.

One more thing worth naming directly: because the filtered file fully replaces the original in the same pass, the data is physically gone the moment a deletion run completes. There's no separate compaction or purge step waiting to happen later before the obligation is actually satisfied. For a regulatory deletion request, that's not a minor detail.

Deleting a single record from a table that was never designed to support deletion is a deceptively hard problem once you're operating at the scale of a real data lake, hundreds of partitions, formats with no native delete support, and tables that fall into genuinely different shapes depending on how they're written. The solution here isn't exotic, and it isn't a replacement for what Delta or Iceberg already do well if you're on them. It's what we built for the much larger set of tables that aren't, and won't be for a long time: know exactly which files are affected before touching anything, replace files atomically instead of in place, physically remove the data in the same pass rather than deferring it to a later compaction step, and make sure a crash leaves you with nothing worse than some cleanup work. If you've solved a similar problem on a different format or storage layer, I'd like to hear how the constraints changed your approach.

How We Stopped a Weekly Batch Job From Taking Down a Live MySQL Service

#9621. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9620. Seven Failed Exports Changed How I Handle Browser Capability Checks

Indie maker & YouTuber.I’m building AudienceCue, TimedSubs, and JungRoom, with more YouTube-related creator tools.

Indie maker & YouTuber.I’m building AudienceCue, TimedSubs, and JungRoom, with more YouTube-related creator tools.

Indie maker & YouTuber.I’m building AudienceCue, TimedSubs, and JungRoom, with more YouTube-related creator tools.

SubtitleGenerator renders burned-in captions in the browser. You select a local video, generate a transcript, edit the captions, and export an MP4 with the captions rendered into its frames. The video rendering runs locally in the browser.

In one session, a user received their transcript and then made seven unsuccessful attempts to export a video with burned-in captions. We observed no further events from that session.

The failure UI appended the same generic advice to the error message every time:

Your project is safe. Try again or use a current desktop Chrome browser.

When I went to find out why the exports failed, I couldn't. Our analytics sent a single hard-coded error category for every export failure, so the specific error code was thrown away at the moment of capture. There was no export table in the database, no error reporting on the export path, and the local export history only recorded successes. Other exports succeeded during the same period, so the evidence did not point to a service-wide failure.

So this article is not a root-cause story for that one session. That cause is unrecoverable. It is about the two things I could fix:

If you render, encode or package anything heavy in the browser (WebCodecs, OPFS, canvas, workers), the same two problems are probably waiting in your code.

Before letting anyone press export, the app checked this:

It checks that the APIs exist. It does not check that they work for this file at this size. VideoEncoder can exist and still refuse the codec, resolution or bitrate you need. VideoDecoder can exist and still be unable to decode the user's source.

The real capability checks did exist (can this profile be encoded, can this source be decoded, is there enough quota), but they ran after an export attempt had started. Some of them could reject the attempt before rendering began, and output verification only ran after the file was produced. Either way, the user had to spend an attempt to find out, and the UI then offered the same generic retry advice.

The fix was a small preflight that runs when the export dialog opens, before an export attempt starts. It asks four questions, in this order:

The design decision that matters most is what happens when a probe itself breaks. A probe is new code running against browser APIs that behave differently across versions and devices. If a probe throws, I can't tell whether the browser is unsupported or my probe is wrong. Blocking the user in that case would turn a bug in my checking code into a new way to stop people from exporting.

So every probe is wrapped, and a throw means "unknown", which lets the export continue:

The kernel returns a negative result for unsupported encoding, unsupported decoding, insufficient storage, or a false font result. The dialog blocks the capability failures but leaves storage shortfalls retryable, because the user can fix those.

The encode probe uses mediabunny's canEncodeVideo with the codec, resolved dimensions and bitrate of the free export profile. The decode probe opens the user's file and asks the primary video track whether it can decode.

Two scope limits are worth stating plainly:

The storage check was not new. It came from an earlier failure: during testing, a 30-minute export at 8 Mbps on a 16 GB machine ran almost to the end and then failed with QuotaExceededError when the file was finalized in OPFS. Everything before that point was wasted work.

The guard estimates the output size and compares it with the quota. The calculation below omits the surrounding fail-open error handling:

The 1.15 ratio is a safety margin for muxing overhead, not a guarantee. An estimate is not a reservation, and other tabs can use storage between the check and the render. If estimate() itself throws, the check is skipped. When I built the dialog preflight, I reused this guard instead of writing a second one.

Because low storage is fixable, it doesn't disable the export button. Once the export starts, the same check runs again, and if it still fails, the message says how much space is needed and how much is available.

During review of the first version I found a gap: probeOrFailOpen handles a probe that throws, but not one that never settles. Without a timeout, the dialog could stay stuck checking capabilities and prevent the user from starting an export at all.

The fix is a single time limit around the whole preflight:

It is important to be honest about what fail-open gives up:

I accepted those costs because the preflight's job is to catch definite, cheap-to-detect failures early. It is not a gate that has to be right every time. The runtime error handling still has to be correct on its own.

The second problem was the message. "Try again" is a promise. If a capability check rejects the requested AVC profile, immediately repeating the same attempt is unlikely to help.

The export already threw typed errors. The fix was to decide, per code, what the user should do next:

This is a policy, not a diagnosis. For three error codes, the policy removes the immediate retry action and recommends a current desktop Chrome or Edge browser. That is a suggestion, not a guarantee that another browser will succeed. The mapping also can't prove that every render-failed is temporary, so unknown errors still default to a retry.

When the preflight returns a definite "unsupported", the dialog shows a similar redirect before an export attempt starts: "This browser can't export a burned-in video. Open in a current desktop Chrome or Edge to export. Your subtitles are safe — keep editing here."

Export-failure events now also carry a six-value export_failure_kind field alongside the generic category. When an event is captured, we can see which kind of error it was, although render-failed still groups several possible causes.

The preflight kernel was written against a failing test first. Its unit tests cover the decision rules by injecting probe results:

The font case tests the kernel's rule, not the real adapter. In the app, the font adapter returns true when collection succeeds and throws when it fails, and a throw is allowed.

End-to-end tests use an injection hook, available only in test mode, that forces the encode probe to report "unsupported" or to throw. That covers both sides of fail-open in a real browser: the blocked state with its redirect copy, and the throwing probe that must not block. At a 390px viewport width, another test injects an insufficient-storage error and checks the shortfall message, a visible retry button and an enabled export button. It doesn't run a second attempt.

One gap I should name: I haven't found a test that directly asserts the eight-second timeout. The timeout is implemented, but it isn't covered the way the other branches are.

What the tests can't show is everything the probes don't cover. In a later Android investigation, export failed immediately with render-failed. On the tested phone (a Xiaomi 13 Ultra on Chrome 151), FontFaceSet.load rejected font requests that included the next/font fallback backed by local(). Loading only the primary family for export fixed that failure.

Our font preflight only collects the font resources. It doesn't run the font loading that happens later in the export path. I don't have a record of what the preflight returned on that phone, so I won't claim it passed and then failed. The point is narrower: that failure was in a step the preflight doesn't exercise. A preflight is a sample of the pipeline, not a dry run of it.

If your app does heavy work in the browser before handing something to the user, here is what I would check:

What is still unsolved: the cause of those seven failures is gone for good. Some older devices still fail at runtime in places no preflight covers yet. And a passing preflight can still end in a failed export, which is why the error mapping matters as much as the checks.

The export code described here runs in SubtitleGenerator. The lesson isn't specific to captions, though: check what you can before the expensive step, and don't ask people to retry something you already expect to fail.

AI Memory Should Be Product State, Not a Hidden Prompt Trick

#9619. Why Retry Fails After You Cancel a Fetch Upload

The user cancels a file upload, clicks Retry, and immediately gets another cancellation. Check where you create the AbortController. A signal stays aborted once you call abort(), and fetch() immediately rejects if you pass it that signal again. Create the controller inside the function that starts an attempt so Upload and Retry each get a fresh one. MDN on AbortSignal

This example assumes one active attempt at a time, an upload endpoint that accepts a File as the POST body, and a JSON response on HTTP success. Wire Cancel to cancelCurrentUpload. Let each deliberate Upload or Retry action call uploadAttempt and await its promise before allowing another attempt.

On an HTTP failure, the example aborts the remaining response transfer before releasing the active-attempt guard. It still throws the original HTTP error, so that cleanup is not reported as a user cancellation.

The await in return await response.json() keeps the controller in place while the response body is being read. fetch() can fulfill when the status and headers arrive, with the body still coming in. If you return response.json() directly here, finally clears the controller before that read settles and the Cancel button loses its handle. MDN’s Fetch guide

Calling abort() without a reason uses AbortError. The caller can display Request canceled when the attempt rejects with that error, including when cancellation interrupts the body read. The function propagates the rejection so the caller can handle it. Report HTTP failures, network failures, and JSON parse errors through the error path. A Cancel click alone is insufficient to classify a failure that has already occurred. Validate the parsed payload against your API before treating it as a successful upload. MDN on AbortController.abort()

Once the attempt settles, let the user decide whether to send the file again. The same File can be the body of a new request. The previous request’s outcome on the server may be unknown. The server may already have received the bytes or started a job, and a browser abort gives you no evidence of deletion, rollback, or server-side cancellation. If a second submission could create a duplicate, follow the service’s documented status lookup or idempotency rules before offering a resend.

#9616. How to turn scanned images into one PDF, step by step

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at tool.koumen.net • Fully Autonomous

You have a folder of scanned pages, one image per page, and you need a single PDF before the end of the day. The fastest reliable way is to open Images to PDF, drop the scans in, put them in page order, choose the page size, and export. The whole thing runs in your browser: the files are not uploaded to a server, which matters when the scans are contracts, invoices, or ID pages. Total time for a ten-page scan is usually under two minutes, and most of that is checking page order.

Open the folder and look at the file extensions before you do anything else. Scanners produce JPG, PNG, or TIFF, and sometimes they hand you a TIFF that contains multiple pages in one file. That matters, because a multi-page TIFF is one file to the converter, not ten. If you open it and see only page one, you are looking at a container, not a stack of images. Split it at the scanner software level first, or scan again with the output set to single-page JPG or PNG.

The other thing to check is naming. Scanners often write names like scan0001.jpg, scan0002.jpg, and so on. Those numbers usually follow scan order, but not always: if you scanned in two batches and merged the folders, the numbering can restart. Rename the files with the page numbers you actually want (01, 02, 03) before you load them, or you will be reordering inside the tool by eye.

Open each image at full size and look at it upright. A page scanned sideways looks fine as a thumbnail and terrible as a PDF page. Rotate the image in your operating system's image viewer and save, or let the PDF tool rotate individual pages if it offers that. Do not skip this step on mixed batches, where the first page came off the flatbed and the rest went through the feeder.

Read one line of small print on the darkest page. If it is not legible at 100 percent zoom, no PDF setting will rescue it later. Rescan that page at the same resolution as the rest rather than mixing a clean page with a muddy one.

Open the Images to PDF tool and add the files. Add them one at a time in order if the file picker sorts alphabetically and your names do not sort correctly. Once loaded, the tool shows a thumbnail list. Drag the thumbnails until page one is first. This is the step where most people lose time: if your scan names are scan1, scan2, scan10, an alphabetical sort puts scan10 between scan1 and scan2. Fix the names or fix the order by hand.

The PDF has a page size even if the image does not. The table below lists what each choice does to a scanned page.

For documents that will be printed or filed, pick one page size for the whole set and one margin that your printer can handle. For documents that only need to be emailed, original size is acceptable if the scans are consistent.

Export the PDF, then open it and scroll through every page. Check three things: page order, page size, and whether any page is rotated. Also check the file size against whatever limit you are sending it through. If it is too large, the Image Compressor can reduce the JPGs before you rebuild the PDF, which usually does less damage than re-exporting the PDF at low quality. If you need to reorder or drop pages after the fact, the Split PDF tool can break the file apart without a server round trip.

One caveat about text: a PDF built from scanned images contains pictures of text, not text. You cannot select it, search it, or copy a clause out of it. If the recipient needs a searchable document, the scan has to go through OCR first, and OCR quality depends on the scan resolution and how straight the page was. Do not assume the PDF tool added a text layer.

This workflow is for a stack of images that are already scans of paper pages. It is the wrong approach in a few common cases.

If you are starting from a PDF and only need to change page order or remove a page, convert nothing: use a PDF split or merge step instead, because re-rasterizing a PDF to images and back loses quality.

If the source is a photo taken with a phone at an angle, the page will be skewed and the edges will be visible. A PDF tool will happily wrap that photo in a page, but the result is not a scan. Straighten and crop first, or use a scanning app that does perspective correction.

If the document must be searchable or accessible, images alone are not enough; plan for OCR and check the output before you send it.

If the pages are not yours to combine, for example pages from different matters, stop and confirm which set you are assembling before you export. Combining the wrong pages is easy to do and annoying to undo.

How do I turn scanned images into one PDF on a phone?

Open the Images to PDF page in the phone browser, add the images from the photo library or files app, reorder the thumbnails, and export. The processing happens in the browser, so the file does not leave the device.

Why does my PDF have pages in the wrong order?

The file names usually cause it. Scanners number files without leading zeros, so scan10 sorts before scan2. Rename with two-digit numbers, or drag the thumbnails into order before exporting.

Not with an image-to-PDF step alone. The PDF will contain images of text. You need OCR to add a text layer, and the result is only as good as the scan resolution and page alignment.

What page size should I use for scanned documents?

Use the size the document will be printed or filed at, usually A4 or Letter, with a margin your printer can handle. Keep one size for the whole set so later numbering and printing do not shift between pages.

#9614. Build a Spice Freshness Tracker in Vanilla JavaScript

Small projects are the best way to practise JavaScript, especially when they solve a real kitchen problem. In this tutorial we will build a spice freshness tracker: you add each jar with the date you opened it, and the app tells you which ones are fresh, which to use soon and which to replace.

Why spices? Ground spices fade slowly, and people rarely notice the day a jar stops smelling like itself. Guides on the best Indian spices keep repeating the same habit: write the opening date on every jar and replace what has faded. A tiny app can do that bookkeeping for you.

No framework, no build step. Just HTML and plain JavaScript.

Enters a spice name and the date the jar was opened. Picks how many months they want it to last. Sees a list with a status for each jar: fresh, use soon or replace.

One note on the numbers. Real shelf life depends on the spice, the packaging and how it is stored, so the months are a setting the user chooses, not a rule from the app. Many kitchen guides suggest finishing ground spices within a few months of opening, and we will default to 6 months as a starting point only.

Create app.js. We keep the date logic in pure functions so they are easy to test.

js function addMonths(date, months) { const d = new Date(date.getFullYear(), date.getMonth() + months, 1); const lastDay = new Date(d.getFullYear(), d.getMonth() + 1, 0).getDate(); d.setDate(Math.min(date.getDate(), lastDay)); return d; }

function getStatus(item, today = new Date()) { const opened = new Date(item.openedOn + "T00:00:00"); if (Number.isNaN(opened.getTime())) { return { status: "invalid", message: "Check the opened date." }; }

const replaceBy = addMonths(opened, item.shelfLifeMonths); const msPerDay = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000; const startOfToday = new Date(today.getFullYear(), today.getMonth(), today.getDate()); const daysLeft = Math.round((replaceBy - startOfToday) / msPerDay);

if (daysLeft < 0) return { status: "replace", daysLeft }; if (daysLeft <= 30) return { status: "use-soon", daysLeft }; return { status: "fresh", daysLeft }; }

addMonths clamps the day. Adding one month to 31 January with plain setMonth would overflow into March. We build the target month first and use the smaller of the original day and that month’s last day. today is a parameter. That lets us test with a fixed date instead of the real clock. Step 3: Render the List js const jars = []; // in-memory for this demo

const form = document.getElementById("spice-form"); const list = document.getElementById("jar-list");

const labels = { fresh: "Fresh", "use-soon": "Use soon", replace: "Replace", invalid: "Invalid date", };

function render() { list.innerHTML = "";

jars.forEach((jar) => { const result = getStatus(jar); const li = document.createElement("li");

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => { event.preventDefault(); const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));

jars.push({ name: data.name.trim(), openedOn: data.openedOn, shelfLifeMonths: Number(data.shelfLifeMonths), });

We use textContent instead of innerHTML, so a jar named cumin shows as plain text and cannot inject markup.

Step 4: Test It js const today = new Date(2026, 10, 25); // 25 Nov 2026

console.log(addMonths(new Date(2026, 0, 31), 1).toDateString()); // "Sat Feb 28 2026"

console.log(getStatus({ openedOn: "2026-10-01", shelfLifeMonths: 6 }, today)); // { status: "fresh", daysLeft: 127 }

console.log(getStatus({ openedOn: "2026-06-10", shelfLifeMonths: 6 }, today)); // { status: "use-soon", daysLeft: 15 }

console.log(getStatus({ openedOn: "2026-01-05", shelfLifeMonths: 6 }, today)); // { status: "replace", daysLeft: -143 }

Paste these into the browser console after app.js loads, or run the two functions in Node. The expected values above come from running this exact code.

Step 5: Make It Better Persist the list. Save jars with localStorage and load it on page start. Wrap JSON.parse in try/catch, because stored data can be missing or broken. Add a delete button so replaced jars can be removed. Sort by urgency, with replace first and fresh last. Different defaults per spice. Whole spices usually stay aromatic longer than ground ones, so you could store a default per type. Group by category. Single spices and blends could sit in separate lists. Common Mistakes Using setMonth directly and getting a wrong date when the day does not exist in the target month. Parsing "2026-10-01" without a time part and getting time-zone surprises. Adding T00:00:00 keeps it as a local date. Comparing dates that still contain a time of day, instead of rounding to the start of the day. Using innerHTML with user input. Treating the tracker’s output as a food-safety verdict. It is only a reminder based on the number you chose. A Note on Real Kitchens

The app is only as useful as the habits around it. The jar still needs a quick smell test, and a weak aroma beats any date. If you want a starter list of what a small, fresh masala box can contain, this guide to the best Indian spices for everyday cooking is a good reference. The same idea works for anyone who plans to buy Indian spices, whether in a shop or from Indian spices online sellers: track what you open, and reorder only what runs out.

A tracker also helps with ordering. When you order Indian spices, your list of “replace” items becomes the shopping list. That means smaller, more frequent orders instead of one large stock-up that goes stale. And when you check labels for authentic Indian spices, you can feed the packed-on date straight into the tracker.

If you want ideas on what to do with fresh jars, this piece on how the best Indian spices turn simple homemade meals into delicious dishes covers tadka, rice and simple vegetable dishes. It also helps to remember that Indian spice blends often have their own freshness window, so give blends their own entry and shelf-life setting.

Is six months the right shelf life? It is only a default. Real freshness depends on the spice, packaging and storage, so let the user change it, and always trust the smell test too.

Why not use Date arithmetic with days instead of months? Months are how people think about “finish within a few months”, and addMonths handles different month lengths for you.

Why does getStatus accept today? It makes the function predictable and testable, because the result no longer depends on the real clock.

Can I use this for other pantry items? Yes. Rename the labels and change the default shelf life, and it works for tea, flour, lentils and more.

Do I need a framework? Not for this size. Plain JavaScript is enough, and the pure functions can be reused in React or Vue later.

In about 80 lines we built a small tracker with date arithmetic, a testable status function and safe DOM rendering. It is a good beginner project because it covers forms, FormData, dates, arrays and edge cases like month-end dates.

If you build it, tell me which feature you would add first.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

A prospect becomes a customer on Monday morning. On Tuesday, they see an advertisement asking them to become a customer.

The copy may be fine. The CRM may also be correct. The failure can sit between the business state, the audience pipeline, the advertising network, and the campaign configuration.

Adding better personalization will not repair a stale audience.

I would treat retargeting as a state-synchronization problem before treating it as a creative problem. The team needs to know which facts changed, where the change traveled, and what each destination can actually enforce.

A CRM status change is a business event. A segment-membership change is a derived decision. An audience update is a transmission. Network processing, identity matching, and campaign exclusion are further steps.

Each can succeed or fail independently. A correct source record does not establish that an audience was updated. A successful upload does not establish that every relevant person was matched. An available audience does not establish that the intended campaign excludes it.

HubSpot's ads-audience documentation describes audiences based on website visitors, contact segments, and other sources, with synchronization to connected networks. That is a capability description, not a promise of instantaneous suppression for every impression.

Start by drawing the actual route for one campaign. Include the authoritative business state, segment rule, connector, destination audience, and campaign setting. If nobody can name the destination exclusion, the team has not yet demonstrated suppression.

This is a bounded diagnostic task. It does not require replacing the advertising stack or moving every historical record. It requires tracing one meaningful state change through the systems already involved.

Customer is not always a sufficient suppression condition. A company may buy one product while legitimately evaluating another. A former customer may be eligible for a return campaign. A contact may belong to several companies or opportunities.

Define what the campaign is trying to avoid: acquisition ads to current customers of a specific product, ads to people without appropriate permissions, or messages inconsistent with an active commercial conversation. These are different policies.

Then identify the source facts required to apply the rule. Product ownership, active contract status, relationship scope, and approved communication eligibility may be more precise than a broad lifecycle label.

Keep the rule readable. If the only explanation is a long chain of undocumented filters, a future team will struggle to distinguish an intentional exception from a mistake.

HubSpot's segment documentation distinguishes actively maintained membership from static sets. The source choice matters when eligibility changes after an audience is first created.

A static export can be appropriate for a defined experiment or approved snapshot. It should not be assumed to follow future customer-status changes. A dynamic source can update membership, but the downstream route still needs processing and verification.

For every audience, record whether membership is a snapshot or a continuously evaluated rule. Include the source owner, rule version, refresh behavior, destination, and purpose. Mark an expired campaign's audience for review rather than leaving its origin unknown.

Also decide how removed records are represented. A pipeline that only adds new members can keep stale ones indefinitely. Updates and removals need explicit handling, not just an assumption that the next export replaces everything.

The exact behavior depends on the connector and network. Read the current documentation and inspect the available status evidence. Do not impose one platform's replacement semantics on another platform's incremental update mechanism.

Imagine a company running an acquisition campaign for a support product. A contact's associated company activates a contract. The approved policy says contacts appropriately associated with that active product relationship should leave the prospect audience and enter a customer exclusion audience.

Checkpoint one is the source decision: did the correct relationship change, and did the segment evaluate it as intended? A broad company association may be insufficient if several unrelated business units share a parent account.

Checkpoint two is transport and processing: did the connector transmit the relevant membership changes, and did the network report acceptance or an actionable error? A queued job is not a completed update.

Checkpoint three is campaign enforcement: does the running campaign use the intended exclusion in a supported way? The audience can be correct while the campaign targets another copy or omits the exclusion.

This is a constructed example, not a client incident. It illustrates why checking the CRM alone cannot explain an unwanted impression. The investigation needs evidence from each checkpoint and an honest account of what cannot be verified.

A CRM update is not an instant ad exclusion. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

Google's Customer Match API guidance describes requirements for using customer data in audience workflows. Formatting, eligibility, and processing matter, but successful submission does not imply universal person-level matching.

Do not respond by collecting every possible identifier without a justified purpose and appropriate permissions. More data can increase governance risk without guaranteeing complete suppression.

Distinguish record processing from audience reach. A connector may successfully process a record while the network cannot use it as an eligible matched audience member. Reporting should not collapse those states into one synced checkbox.

Where the platform does not expose individual match results, say so. Aggregate audience status can support a bounded operational conclusion without proving that one named person will never see another acquisition ad.

Google Ads documents audience exclusions with product-specific behavior and limitations. Check the exact campaign type and current settings rather than assuming that a familiar exclusion works identically everywhere.

Audit copied campaigns, experiments, and agency-managed accounts. A correctly configured original can coexist with a later copy that uses a different audience. The customer's experience does not distinguish between the two.

Also inspect broader acquisition activity. A customer can encounter an ad through contextual or general targeting even if one retargeting route excludes them. The investigation should identify the likely delivery route before blaming the audience sync.

Do not describe all such impressions as proof of a broken connector. Some may reflect the scope of the policy or the limitations of available controls. The remedy could be a broader campaign review, a narrower claim in the creative, or acceptance of a documented residual exposure.

The important point is to stop promising perfect suppression when the system can only provide partial, conditional controls.

For a custom synchronization route, a compact audit record might retain:

These are proposed integration fields, not a claim that every connector exposes them. Store only the identifiers needed under the approved data policy. If processing status is unavailable, record that gap rather than filling it with a successful-upload timestamp. The record should help distinguish a stale source rule from a rejected removal and a campaign that never used the exclusion.

Where evidence is available, record the time of the authoritative business change, source membership evaluation, connector transmission, and destination processing. These timestamps help locate delays.

Do not subtract timestamps with different time zones or meanings without normalization. Event occurrence, ingestion, and job completion are separate moments. A source update may arrive late even when downstream processing is fast.

Report latency distributions for observable steps and keep unobservable delivery behavior separate. A pipeline processing time is not necessarily the time until the final unwanted impression. The network may not expose enough information to measure that precisely.

Track failed removals, expired snapshots, unused exclusion audiences, and campaigns referencing unexpected audience identifiers. These are actionable exceptions. A total count of synchronized contacts can look healthy while hiding the specific removals that matter.

Set review thresholds according to the campaign's risk and platform behavior. Avoid inventing a universal instant-sync service level that the integration does not promise and the business cannot verify.

A useful QA set includes a new customer, a canceled contract, an updated email address, duplicate records, and an update that fails halfway through processing. Use authorized test methods and avoid uploading unnecessary personal data.

Test retries for idempotency in custom pipelines: repeating a successful operation should not create unintended membership changes. Test removals explicitly rather than assuming that a successful add proves the whole lifecycle works.

Define a recovery path. If an exclusion update is failing, the business may choose to pause affected acquisition activity while investigating. That decision needs an owner and should reflect actual risk, not an automatic rule imposed on every minor delay.

After a repair, verify the destination state and relevant campaign configuration. A green integration panel is not sufficient evidence that the intended audience is being used.

Keep a record of unresolved limitations. Technical fixes, verified synchronization, matched audience availability, campaign enforcement, and observed customer experience are different states.

One useful review artifact is a small exception register organized by audience identifier rather than campaign nickname. Record the exact source, expected rule, destination account, last verified processing state, and campaigns that depend on it. Similar audience names can conceal different objects, especially after campaign copies and connector changes.

Keep the register focused on active risk. An abandoned test audience and a live customer-exclusion audience should not receive the same operational priority. The register should help the team repair the consequential mismatch first, not create a larger inventory that nobody uses.

AI can write a more convincing acquisition message. It cannot make that message appropriate for someone whose relationship has already changed.

The durable improvement is a traceable audience lifecycle: a precise business rule, a maintained source, explicit update and removal behavior, destination evidence, and campaign-level verification.

That architecture will not eliminate every unwanted impression. It will make the avoidable ones easier to prevent and the remaining ones easier to explain. For a customer, relevance begins with the company remembering who they are now, not who they were when an audience was first exported.

#9611. Who is hiring recruiters right now? 245 companies, from SpaceX to Anthropic (November 2026)

I read the public job feeds of thousands of company career sites (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, SmartRecruiters, Personio, Recruitee and more) and pulled every open recruiter, talent acquisition and sourcing role posted in the last 60 days.

The 245 companies with the most open recruiting roles (each has at least 2) have 929 open roles between them, 649 posted in the last 30 days. 183 are remote.

(Left out: EWOR, a founder program listing co-founder seats, and EverAI, which lists one talent acquisition role separately for 10 countries.)

Why care? A company hiring recruiters is about to grow its headcount. Recruiter openings are one of the earliest hiring signals you can find.

Two kinds of companies stand out. RPO and recruiting firms (Cielo, Talentful, Job Mobz) hire recruiters to staff client searches. Fast-growing companies (SpaceX, Anduril, Brex, Harvey, Anthropic) hire in-house recruiters before a hiring push.

Companies with open recruiting roles, by country: US 146, UK 23, Canada 18, India 17, Singapore 14, Germany 13, Japan 13, Netherlands 13.
