#9609. Space-to-Ground Connectivity: Implementing NB-NTN in Consumer Devices

Antenna Engineer thriving at the intersection of electromagnetic innovation and high-volume consumer technology

Antenna Engineer thriving at the intersection of electromagnetic innovation and high-volume consumer technology

Antenna Engineer thriving at the intersection of electromagnetic innovation and high-volume consumer technology

Cellular coverage ends where the map gets interesting: hiking trails, open water, disaster zones. Satellite direct-to-device fills that gap, and the first use cases are deliberately narrow: emergency SOS, remote tracking, short messaging. Narrow is fine. When someone is lost with no bars, a 160-character message to a satellite is everything.

The standard path runs through 3GPP Release 17, which adapted NB-IoT protocols for non-terrestrial networks. NB-NTN gives device makers a defined air interface instead of a proprietary one. But the standard only describes the conversation. It doesn't solve the physics of having it from a wrist.

Smartwatches are the hardest NTN platform in consumer electronics. The ground plane is tiny, the battery holds a few hundred milliamp-hours, and the antenna sits against a human body that absorbs RF for a living. Everything that follows is about those three constraints.

This article examines the physical-layer realities, RF front-end architectures, and empirical link budgets required to establish and maintain a 3GPP Release 17 NB-NTN connection directly from a wrist-worn form factor.

Standard satellite downlinks utilize Circular Polarization (typically RHCP) to eliminate Faraday rotation effects in the ionosphere and to mitigate orientation-dependent cross-polarization fading. Generating high-purity circular polarization (axial ratio < 3 dB) across a hemisphere requires either:

Dual-point fed stacked patch antennas, or

Multi-arm crossed planar inverted-F antennas (PIFAs).

In a 42-46 mm chassis  accommodating a patch antenna thick enough to achieve usable bandwidth at S-band (e.g., 3GPP Band n256: 2170–2200 MHz DL, 1980–2010 MHz UL) or L-band (Band n255: 1525–1559 MHz DL, 1626.5–1660.5 MHz UL) is physically prohibited by the Z-height consumed by the OLED panel, touch sensor, logic board, and battery.

Consequently, wearable implementations frequently make a deliberate trade-off: implement a linear (or imperfectly elliptical) radiator and accept a theoretical 3 dB polarization mismatch loss against the satellite's circular wave. Real-world axial ratios on wearable antennas typically degrade to > 8 dB off-boresight, meaning the front-end budget must explicitly absorb this 3 dB hit rather than burning PCB volume on complex phase-shifting networks

At 2 GHz, the free-space wavelength (λ) is 150 mm. A resonant half-wavelength dipole requires 75 mm. A typical watch PCB provides a continuous conductive chassis of only 30 to 40 mm (0.2λ to 0.26λ). Because the ground plane cannot support resonant return currents, the entire metal perimeter of the watch—including the exterior bezel and titanium or aluminum mid-frame—must serve as the radiator.

A common implementation is a chassis-integrated slot antenna or multi-segment inverted-F antenna (IFA) where mechanical isolation breaks in the frame act as tuning apertures. In free-space, these designs can achieve peak gains of +1 to +2 dBi. However, once placed on the body, biological loading reduces the total radiated power (TRP) and total isotropic sensitivity (TIS) significantly.

Human tissue acts as a high-permittivity capacitive load. Placing the ground plane within 82 mm of the epidermis causes two primary degradations:

Accounting for chassis limitations and body proximity, the realized on-wrist antenna gain (Gr) at low elevation angles (20° to 30°) typically falls between -3 and -6 dBi.

The defining number in NTN work is path loss: more than 160 dB between a wrist-worn device and a low-earth-orbit satellite. Every dB in that budget is contested. Antenna gain, front-end losses, and transmit power all get spent against it, and there's no margin to waste.

The power amplifier is where the budget meets the battery. The link needs enough effective radiated power to close, but the PA has to deliver it without overheating the device or draining a 300 to 500 mAh battery in minutes. PA efficiency isn't a nice-to-have here. It's the difference between a feature and a demo.

Link margin management is the operational answer. Under foliage, body blocking, or bad orientation, the device trades data rate for stability: lower-order modulation, more repetitions, narrower bandwidth. The link gets slower so it can stay alive. Designing that fallback ladder, and deciding when to climb it, is core NTN firmware work.

To evaluate feasibility, we analyze an uplink and downlink link budget for a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite at a 600 km orbital altitude, observed at a 30° elevation angle.

Slant Range and Free Space Path Loss (FSPL)

The slant distance d between the wearable terminal and the satellite is calculated as:

d = sqrt(R_E^2 * sin^2(θ) + 2 * R_E * h + h^2) - R_E * sin(θ)

FSPL = 20log10(d) + 20log10(f) + 20*log10(4π / c)

At an S-band uplink frequency of f = 2.0 GHz:

FSPL = 20log10(1.093 x 10^6) + 20log10(2.0 x 10^9) - 147.55 ≈ 159.27 dB

At S-band downlink (2.18 GHz), FSPL ≈ 160.02 dB.

The following budget reflects a 3GPP Release 17 NB-IoT NTN deployment operating with a single-tone allocation to concentrate power spectral density (PSD).

Under line-of-sight conditions with single-carrier narrowband transmission (3.75 kHz spacing), the uplink closes with a +9.94 dB margin.

However, if the user turns their body so that torso shadowing occurs (inducing an additional 10 to 15 dB attenuation), the link margin falls below zero. The modem must drop down the Modulation and Coding Scheme (MCS) ladder and engage repetition coding (N_rep = 4, 8, 16 ... 128), as standardized in 3GPP TS 36.211.

While repetitions restore the link by accumulating energy over time, they linearly scale transmit time, directly impacting the watch's battery:

Where P_DC is the DC power drawn by the PA. At +23 dBm RF output and a conservative 28% PAE, the front-end pulls approximately 714 mW. Running N_rep = 32 transitions a short transmission from a 200 ms burst into a multi-second transmission, rapidly depleting cell capacity.

LEO satellites move fast, and that motion shows up as Doppler shift. The device has to track the frequency offset continuously and compensate, or the signal slides out of the receiver's window mid-message. Doppler compensation isn't optional in NTN. It's part of the baseband's job description.

The watch's own GNSS receiver helps more than you'd expect. Position and velocity from GPS give the modem a head start on satellite acquisition and synchronization: it knows which satellite should be overhead and roughly what Doppler to expect. Sensor fusion between GNSS and the NTN stack shortens the search and saves battery.

Then there's the wrist itself. Antenna impedance changes as the wrist moves, as skin contact changes, as the strap tightens. Dynamic impedance matching adjusts the antenna tuning in real time against body loading. Without it, the carefully tuned lab performance evaporates the moment someone actually wears the device.

Validation cannot rely on standard terrestrial multipath chambers. The long propagation delays (10 to 40 ms) and dynamic orbital trajectories require specialized emulation methods.

Testing must use hand and wrist phantoms formulated to mimic human tissue dielectric properties per CTIA OTA Test Plan standards:

Relative permittivity (εr): 35 to 42 between 1.5 and 2.2 GHz.

Measurements must capture three-dimensional radiation performance:

Upper Hemisphere Total Radiated Power (UH-TRP): Quantifying total energy emitted into the skyward hemisphere (2π steradians), rather than standard total spherical integration (4π), since power absorbed by or directed through the arm does not contribute to the satellite link.

Upper Hemisphere Total Isotropic Sensitivity (UH-TIS): Evaluating the receiver's sensitivity specifically against signals originating above the artificial horizon.

Human-in-the-loop testing is the part teams underestimate. Phantom wrists, tissue-equivalent arms loaded with the device, let you measure total isotropic sensitivity and total radiated power across arm positions without booking field time. Field testing still matters, hiking trails and open sky, but the phantom catches the regressions first.

Two test dimensions deserve their own plans. The wrist-to-sky geometry changes everything: a hiker's raised arm and a runner's swinging wrist are different RF environments, and emergency use has its own posture. Multi-satellite handover testing verifies session continuity as the device moves between satellites, because a dropped session during an SOS is the failure that matters most.

SAR compliance constrains the uplink directly. High-power satellite bursts have to stay within RF exposure limits, which caps how aggressively the device can push power to close a marginal link. The regulatory team isn't a downstream reviewer here. They're a design input.

The sky-view user experience is a design problem most cellular engineers never face. The user has to orient the watch toward the satellite, which means the UI has to guide them: where to point, when the satellite passes, how long the window lasts. An SOS feature nobody can aim is a failed feature.

Battery budgeting closes the loop. Deep-sleep modes and wake-up signals have to be tuned around satellite paging latency, which is nothing like cellular paging. Every milliamp spent listening for a satellite that isn't there is battery the SOS won't have later.

The trajectory points from NB-NTN toward 5G RedCap NTN: higher bandwidth, richer wearable applications, the same physics. The antenna and link-budget disciplines don't change. The data rates do.

There's a reasonable future where satellite-to-wearable becomes a standard outdoor safety feature, as unremarkable as GPS is today. Getting there runs through the unglamorous work: antenna-chassis co-design, software-defined tuning, and validation that treats the wrist as part of the RF system.

Direct-to-satellite connectivity in a smartwatch cannot be solved through brute-force RF power scaling. Operating at the limits of battery capacity and chassis volume requires balanced physical compromises:

Closing this link demands deep co-design across mechanical packaging, structural RF, antenna tuning, and baseband firmware. Wearable NTN terminals demonstrate that even highly constrained link budgets can be made operational through targeted RF architecture and disciplined physical integration.

The watch is the smallest satellite terminal ever mass-produced. Making it work took every dB the physics allowed and a few the engineering created. That's the job.

Antenna Engineer thriving at the intersection of electromagnetic innovation and high-volume consumer technology

#9608. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. #9606. Your Predictive AI Saw the Failure Coming. Nobody Changed Anything.

There is something strange about building an AI system that can predict a machine failure three days before it happens, only to watch that machine break down anyway.

The model did what it was designed to do. It analysed sensor readings, identified an unusual pattern, calculated a risk score and generated an alert. From a machine learning perspective, that might look like a successful outcome.

But from the perspective of a manufacturing business, the result is very different.

Production stopped. Orders were delayed. Maintenance teams were called in unexpectedly. Spare parts had to be arranged urgently. The company lost valuable production hours, and someone eventually asked a question that the AI dashboard could not answer.

If the system knew this was coming, why didn't we prevent it?

I think this is one of the most important problems facing predictive AI today. We have become increasingly good at building models that identify patterns, estimate probabilities and forecast possible outcomes. But predicting an event and changing the conditions that lead to that event are two very different engineering problems.

In manufacturing, the difference can be expensive. A predictive maintenance model might identify a 90% probability of equipment failure within the next 72 hours. That sounds impressive. But what happens next? Does a maintenance ticket get created? Does someone verify the prediction? Is the required replacement part available? Can production be rescheduled? Does a human need to approve shutting down an expensive machine?

If none of these things happens, the prediction remains an observation. And observations do not repair machines. In my view, the next important step in enterprise AI is not simply building models that predict more accurately. It is building intelligent systems that can translate predictions into decisions, coordinate the required actions and verify whether those actions actually changed the outcome.

That is where predictive intelligence becomes operational intelligence.

Let's consider a manufacturing facility operating several industrial machines across multiple production lines.

One of its critical machines contains vibration sensors, temperature sensors and pressure monitoring equipment. These sensors continuously generate information about operating conditions. The data is collected and analysed by a predictive AI system.

For several weeks, the machine has operated normally. Then the model begins identifying a combination of unusual patterns. Vibration levels are gradually increasing, operating temperature is slightly above its normal range, and pressure readings are becoming less stable.

Individually, none of these signals necessarily indicates an immediate failure. Together, however, they may indicate a developing mechanical problem. The model calculates a high risk of equipment failure within the next 72 hours. Consider the following illustrative prediction:

The prediction is useful. It allows the maintenance team to investigate before the equipment fails. However, the prediction itself does not answer several operational questions.

Is the machine actually experiencing a mechanical defect, or is the sensor producing unreliable readings? Is a technician available? Is the replacement component in stock? Can production temporarily move to another machine? Will stopping the equipment now create a larger operational problem than continuing to run it?

These questions cannot be answered by a failure probability alone. This is where many predictive AI implementations encounter difficulties. The model produces an output, but the organisation has not built the decision-making process required to act on it.

The prediction reaches a dashboard. Someone receives an email. A notification appears in a monitoring system, and then nothing happens.

The missing component is not necessarily a better machine learning algorithm. It is the operational decision layer connecting intelligence to execution.

When a predictive AI project does not deliver the expected business outcome, it is tempting to immediately question the model's accuracy.

Sometimes that is justified. Models can generate false positives, miss developing faults or perform poorly when operating conditions change. But not every failed prediction-to-action workflow is a modelling problem.

There are several other reasons why an organisation can have a technically successful predictive system and still experience preventable failures.

One of the most overlooked problems is ownership. An AI system generates an alert and sends it to a maintenance dashboard. The maintenance team assumes the production supervisor will review it. The supervisor expects the maintenance manager to approve the intervention. The maintenance manager is waiting for a technical assessment.

Everyone knows about the prediction, but nobody owns the next decision. This is an organisational problem disguised as a technology problem.

Every actionable prediction needs a defined owner. That does not mean the AI should independently decide everything. It means the system should know who is responsible for reviewing the recommendation, who can approve an intervention and what should happen if nobody responds within the required timeframe.

A prediction without an assigned decision owner is simply another notification competing for attention.

A model might predict that a machine has a 90% probability of failure within three days. It does not automatically know whether the factory can afford to stop that machine immediately.

Manufacturing operations involve dependencies. A machine may be connected to several downstream production processes. Shutting it down could affect an entire production schedule.

There may also be constraints involving spare parts, technicians, supplier availability, production commitments and safety procedures.

The probability of failure is the only one input into the decision.

A useful predictive system must consider the operational consequences of different actions. Sometimes, immediate intervention is the right decision. Sometimes a controlled inspection is more appropriate. In other cases, the business may need to adjust production before maintenance can take place.

This is why I distinguish predictive intelligence from decision intelligence. Predictive intelligence estimates what might happen. Decision intelligence helps determine what should happen next, considering the available evidence and business constraints.

False positives can quietly damage an otherwise promising AI implementation.

Imagine a maintenance team receiving ten high-risk alerts in one week. They investigate each one, but eight turn out to be harmless operating variations. The next time the system raises an alert, the team may not respond with the same urgency.

This is a familiar problem in monitoring systems. When alerts repeatedly fail to produce useful outcomes, people begin treating them as background noise.

The solution is not simply to increase the confidence threshold. A higher threshold might reduce false positives, but it could also cause the model to miss failures that develop gradually.

Instead, the organisation needs to understand the cost of different prediction errors. A false positive and a false negative do not necessarily have the same business consequences.

A false positive might result in an unnecessary inspection. A false negative could result in equipment damage, production interruption or a safety incident. The decision policy should reflect those differences.

There is another problem that becomes particularly important when AI predictions are connected to automated workflows. A prediction is based on information available at a particular point in time. But manufacturing conditions continue changing.

Suppose the model predicts a high failure probability at 9:00 AM. The maintenance team receives the alert at 9:10 AM. By 10:00 AM, a technician has already inspected the equipment and replaced a damaged component.

If the original prediction remains active, an automated workflow could still create a maintenance ticket or recommend shutting down the machine.

The model was not necessarily wrong. The underlying situation changed.

This is why predictions need timestamps, data freshness indicators and explicit validity periods. An AI system should not treat an old prediction as a permanent instruction. Before an action is executed, the system should verify whether the conditions that justified that action still exist.

I believe the more interesting architecture is not one where a machine learning model simply sends alerts to another application.

It is one where prediction, evaluation, decision-making, approval, execution and verification operate as connected stages.

The important detail is that the predictive model does not directly control the entire workflow.

Each component has a defined responsibility.

The data collection layer provides observations. The validation layer checks whether those observations are usable. The predictive model estimates risk. The decision intelligence layer evaluates possible interventions. The approval mechanism ensures that authorised people retain control over consequential decisions. The execution layer carries out approved actions, and the verification layer checks whether the expected result actually occurred.

This separation matters because a prediction is not an instruction, and an instruction is not proof of execution. A system that keeps these concepts separate is much easier to operate, audit and improve.

Let's return to our manufacturing example.

The model has identified a 90% failure probability within 72 hours. Instead of immediately sending a generic alert, the decision layer evaluates several possible interventions.

These are illustrative options, not universal maintenance recommendations. Actual decisions must consider equipment specifications, safety procedures, engineering assessments and the consequences of failure.

The decision layer can evaluate the available information and recommend an appropriate next step. For instance, it might determine that an inspection should happen within 12 hours because the prediction is significant, the machine is operationally critical, and the required technician is available.

The recommendation can then be routed to the appropriate maintenance manager. This is much more useful than simply displaying a red warning on a dashboard.

The system is no longer asking someone to interpret an isolated probability. It is presenting a decision supported by evidence, constraints and a proposed course of action.

One mistake I would avoid is allowing a model's confidence score to become the entire decision policy.

A 95% confidence score does not automatically mean an action should be executed. It also does not mean that a 65% prediction should be ignored. The meaning of a probability depends on the model's calibration, the quality of its input data, the event being predicted and the consequences of acting or not acting.

Machine A is relatively inexpensive and has a backup available. Machine B is a critical production asset with no immediate replacement. A similar predicted failure probability could justify different interventions because the operational consequences are different. The decision layer should consider at least four dimensions:

Probability: How likely is the predicted event, and how reliable is the model's probability estimate?

Time: How soon could the event occur, and how long does the organisation need to respond?

Impact: What would happen if the event occurred, and what would be the consequences of intervention?

Feasibility: Does the organisation have the people, equipment, spare parts and operational flexibility required to act?

The result should be a decision supported by multiple sources of information, rather than an automated action triggered by a single threshold.

Let's look at how a simple decision layer might work in Python. The following example is deliberately simplified. It demonstrates how a system can combine a model's prediction with operational context to produce a recommendation. It is not a production-ready maintenance controller, and the thresholds would need to be validated against real equipment and business requirements.

There are a few important design decisions here.

First, invalid sensor data prevents the system from treating the prediction as reliable. A model can produce a probability even when the underlying observations are incomplete or corrupted. The decision layer must not confuse a numerical output with trustworthy evidence.

Second, a safety alert takes precedence over the ordinary predictive workflow. Safety-critical procedures should not be replaced by a model's recommendation.

Third, resource availability affects the recommended action. A system that recommends replacing a component without checking whether the component exists is not providing a complete operational decision.

Finally, the code returns a recommendation rather than directly controlling the machine.

In a real manufacturing environment, the recommendation would pass through an authorisation process before any consequential intervention took place.

There is a temptation to connect predictive models directly to execution systems and describe the result as autonomous manufacturing.

I would be careful with that approach. Not every prediction should trigger an automatic action. Some interventions are reversible and low risk. Others can affect equipment safety, production continuity or expensive assets.

A sensible architecture should distinguish between actions based on their potential impact.

The exact boundaries depend on the equipment and operating environment. The objective is not to remove people from every decision. It is to ensure that people spend their time on decisions that genuinely require human judgment, while predictable and low-risk activities can be handled through controlled automation.

AI should reduce operational friction, not introduce a new category of uncontrolled risk.

This is where I see an interesting opportunity for AI agents. Traditional predictive maintenance systems usually focus on identifying abnormal conditions and generating recommendations. AI agents could extend that capability by coordinating the different systems involved in responding to a prediction.

Imagine an agent receiving a validated equipment-risk event.

It could retrieve the machine's maintenance history, check the availability of replacement components, inspect the production schedule, identify available technicians and prepare a proposed maintenance plan.

It could then present the recommendation to the maintenance manager with supporting evidence. Once approved, the workflow could create the maintenance ticket, reserve the required component and notify the relevant teams.

But there is an important architectural distinction here. The agent should coordinate the workflow, not become the unquestioned authority over every action.

The maintenance system should remain authoritative for work-order status. The inventory system should remain authoritative for spare-part availability. The production scheduling system should remain authoritative for approved schedules.

The agent should not invent a spare-part reservation, assume a technician has accepted an assignment or claim that maintenance has been completed simply because it submitted a request. Every external action needs a verifiable outcome. A practical workflow could look like this:

Notice the difference between steps eight and nine.

Executing an action does not prove that the action succeeded. The system must verify the result using the authoritative external application.

If the maintenance API times out after receiving a request, the agent should not blindly create another work order. It should reconcile the operation against the maintenance system before retrying.

This is particularly important in multi-system manufacturing environments where a single intervention can involve inventory, maintenance, scheduling and procurement.

A mature predictive intelligence system must be designed for incorrect predictions.

Even a well-performing model will encounter uncertainty. Equipment conditions change, sensors fail, operating patterns shift, and previously unseen situations emerge.

Scenario one: The prediction was correct, and the intervention prevented a failure.

The maintenance team inspected the equipment, identified a developing fault and replaced the affected component. The system should record the original prediction, the evidence supporting it, the intervention and the subsequent equipment condition.

Scenario two: The prediction was incorrect.

The maintenance team inspected the machine and found no mechanical defect. This should not automatically be treated as a useless prediction. The organisation needs to understand why the model raised the alert. Was there an unusual operating condition? Was the sensor noisy? Did the model confuse a temporary production change with a developing fault?

Scenario three: The prediction was correct, but nobody acted.

This is perhaps the most revealing outcome. The model identified a genuine problem, but the intervention failed because the alert was not reviewed, resources were unavailable, or the approval process took too long.

If the organisation measures only model accuracy, it may never identify this operational failure.

This is why I believe prediction outcomes and intervention outcomes must be measured separately.

A model can be accurate while the overall system remains ineffective.

One of the biggest mistakes in enterprise AI is evaluating success using model metrics alone.

Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score and AUC are useful for understanding model performance. But they do not tell the complete business story.

A manufacturing organisation also needs operational metrics.

Here are the measurements I would prioritise.

I would also introduce a metric that connects model performance with operational execution:

Prediction-to-intervention conversion rate.

This measures the proportion of actionable predictions that result in a completed, appropriate intervention.

For example, suppose a system generates 100 actionable predictions during a reporting period.

The prediction-to-intervention conversion rate is 48%.

That does not mean the remaining 52 predictions were necessarily failures. Some may have been false positives, some may have become irrelevant after conditions changed, and others may have been rejected for legitimate operational reasons.

The important thing is to understand why each prediction did or did not lead to action.

A useful system should preserve that history rather than treating every unexecuted recommendation as the same type of failure.

There is another area where predictive AI projects can become misleading: return on investment.

Suppose an organisation claims that its predictive maintenance system prevented 500 hours of downtime.

That sounds valuable, but how was the figure calculated?

Would the equipment definitely have failed during those hours? Was the maintenance intervention responsible for avoiding the downtime? Could the same maintenance have happened through an existing preventive maintenance schedule?

These questions matter. Avoided downtime is difficult to measure because the failure that did not happen is not directly observable. A more credible evaluation should compare outcomes against a baseline, account for production conditions and avoid attributing every improvement to AI. A simple financial model might look like this:

The numbers should be based on actual business records wherever possible.

For a rigorous evaluation, organisations can compare similar assets, use historical maintenance records and account for differences in operating conditions. Where feasible, controlled pilots or phased rollouts can help estimate the incremental value of the AI intervention.

The objective is not to produce the largest possible ROI number. It is to establish whether the system genuinely improves operational performance.

There is one more component that I think deserves much more attention. Most predictive AI discussions focus on feeding sensor data into a model and generating a prediction. But the system also needs to learn from what happens after the prediction.

Did the technician confirm the suspected fault? Was the recommended component actually replaced? Did the machine return to normal operating conditions? Did the equipment fail despite the intervention?

These outcomes provide important information. However, not every outcome should automatically become a new training label.

For example, if a maintenance intervention prevents a predicted failure, the organisation cannot simply conclude that the original prediction was false because no failure occurred. The intervention itself may have changed the outcome.

This is a counterfactual problem. The system must distinguish between:

A useful feedback architecture should connect the original prediction with the actual intervention and subsequent equipment observations. It should also preserve the model version, feature data, decision policy version and timestamps associated with the original decision.

That makes it possible to investigate not only whether the model was right, but whether the complete operational process worked as intended.

If I were designing a predictive intelligence platform for a manufacturing environment, I would avoid treating the machine learning model as the centre of the entire system.

The model is important, but it is one component within a much larger decision architecture. I would prioritise five design principles.

1. Make every prediction actionable and traceable.

A prediction should include the equipment identifier, model version, probability estimate, prediction horizon, supporting evidence, timestamp and validity period. It should also identify the operational owner responsible for reviewing it.

2. Separate prediction from authorisation.

The model can recommend an action, but the system's policy layer should determine whether that action is permitted. High-impact decisions should require appropriate human approval.

3. Connect predictions to authoritative operational systems.

Inventory, maintenance, procurement and production scheduling systems should remain the sources of truth for their respective information. AI agents can coordinate these systems without pretending to replace their authority.

4. Verify execution instead of trusting acknowledgements.

A submitted maintenance request is not a completed maintenance operation. A reserved component is not an installed component. Every important transition should be verified against the relevant system.

5. Measure operational outcomes, not just model performance.

The organisation should understand how predictions affect intervention time, downtime, repair costs, equipment reliability and production continuity.

These principles are not limited to manufacturing. They apply to predictive systems in logistics, energy, healthcare operations, financial risk and infrastructure management.

Whenever an AI system predicts a future event, the next engineering challenge is deciding what should happen because of that prediction.

We often describe predictive AI as technology that helps organisations see what is coming.

I think that description is incomplete. Seeing a problem before it happens is valuable, but it does not automatically change the outcome. A warning that arrives too late, reaches the wrong person or cannot be translated into an approved action may have very little operational value.

The next generation of predictive intelligence systems needs to close the gap between prediction and execution. That does not mean giving AI unrestricted authority to make decisions. It means building the architecture, policies, integrations and verification mechanisms that allow intelligent systems to support real operational decisions responsibly.

For manufacturing, that could mean identifying equipment deterioration earlier, coordinating maintenance resources, reducing emergency interventions and improving production planning.

For enterprise AI more broadly, it means moving beyond systems that simply tell us what might happen towards systems that help us decide what to do next.

And perhaps that is the question we should be asking when evaluating the success of predictive AI.

Not simply whether the model predicted the failure correctly. But whether the organisation was able to do something useful with that prediction. Because an AI system that sees a failure coming but cannot help anyone prevent it has only completed half the job.

The real value of predictive intelligence begins when a prediction changes a decision, and that decision changes an outcome.

#9604. Rs 1.98 crore fintech hack: Navi Mumbai Police trace a home VPN node in Chennai

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at igrs.xyz

Navi Mumbai Cyber Police say a Rs 1.98 crore fintech intrusion ran from Hong Kong through VPN nodes hosted in a Chennai home. A second case at a digital bank and a push by banks against pre-authorised payouts show how exposed payment plumbing has become.

Navi Mumbai Cyber Police have arrested an electrical and electronics engineer in Chennai in a case where about Rs 1.98 crore was diverted from a fintech company by breaking into its server and manipulating its payment gateway, according to a Free Press Journal report updated on 25 November. Police say the intrusion was carried out from Hong Kong. The attackers reached the company's electronic ledger and its bank-linked payment gateway without valid credentials and pushed money into several bank accounts. The FIR was registered at Navi Mumbai Cyber Police Station in October 2026 and the arrest was made on 18 November.

The arrested man is not accused of writing the attack. Police allege he set up VPN nodes at his home and made them available to associates abroad, and that he was paid in cryptocurrency and through other digital channels. Investigators traced him through IP addresses linked to the bank transactions, email IDs and account details. They seized a laptop, a router, a Raspberry Pi single-board computer, a memory card and a phone, and say more than Rs 1 crore has been frozen in various accounts. The fintech company has not been named.

A separate case from the same city shows the pattern is wider. FPJ reported on 24 November that between 10 and 15 November about Rs 1.74 crore was moved out of 215 customers' accounts at a Navi Mumbai-headquartered digital payments bank, using what police called a technical loophole in one of its mobile applications. The money went into 322 internal accounts and Rs 1.56 crore was then sent to other banks in 523 transactions. The bank's anti-fraud unit flagged it on 14 November, its information security team traced two IP addresses, and it refunded all 215 customers on 17 November. The bank filed complaints on the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal on 20 November and with police on 21 November, invoking Sections 318(4), 61(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita along with IT Act provisions. It also informed RBI, CERT-In, MHA and RBI's DAKSH portal. No arrest had been reported in that case. We covered it in one paragraph in this morning's India Cyber Brief.

These cases land in a month when regulators and banks are openly worried about machine-to-machine payment channels. On 4 November I4C's threat analytics unit and CERT-In issued a joint advisory warning that financially motivated attackers, using AI agents, were compromising disbursement systems and payment APIs at banks, NBFCs and fintechs, and moving multi-crore sums through mule accounts over IMPS and NEFT before deleting logs, PSU Watch reported. MediaNama reported that RBI followed with a confidential advisory asking banks to keep an inventory of API clients, whitelist beneficiaries, add maker-checker or out-of-band approval for API debits and set per-transaction and daily limits.

On 25 November Elets BFSI, citing The Economic Times, reported that banks have asked I4C and RBI to curb "pre-authorisation" arrangements, under which an NBFC's own system pushes payment instructions into bank rails and the bank pays out in bulk without a login or OTP. Bankers fear that an attacker inside an NBFC could create fake loans to mule accounts or change a genuine borrower's bank details.

Analysis: The Navi Mumbai arrest is useful because it shows the human layer behind a "foreign" intrusion. Operators abroad need Indian-looking network exits so that their traffic passes IP allow-lists and fraud scoring. A home internet connection with a small always-on device is enough to provide that, and the person renting it out becomes the traceable link, much as mule account holders are for the money.

Analysis: Police have not published the sections in the Rs 1.98 crore case. The IT Act and BNSS entries above are our reading of what may apply, not reported charges. Whether renting out a VPN node amounts to abetment or conspiracy will depend on what the accused knew, which is for the court to decide.

Police say the Chennai arrest may connect to other cases, including digital arrest frauds under investigation, and the overseas operators are still to be identified. On the policy side, RBI's draft directions on preventive safeguards for electronic banking transactions are open for comments until 14 December 2026, per Elets BFSI, and the banks' push against pre-authorised NBFC payouts could change how fintech disbursements work.

Originally published on IGRS — Intel Grid Research Station. Free OSINT tools and investigation guides for India: igrs.xyz.

#9601. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

Sounds like you're biased for Grammarly. Not really that informative if you're already leaning towards one to begin with. Still, it was an interesting read. Tell me, do you use Grammarly with your day-to-day writing/blogging?

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9599. What Couples Married For 40 Years Do When Life Gets Hard

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

“Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”

Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:

The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

#9594. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9593. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

#9589. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9582. One Familiar Item Of Clothing Scored Lowest for Intelligence — Can You Guess Which?

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.

Of the six types of clothing the researchers compared, track pants also received the lowest average ratings for trustworthiness.

Blouses topped the rankings for intelligence and trustworthiness but scored near the bottom for confidence.

Short skirts showed almost the reverse pattern, scoring near the top for confidence and lower than long skirts on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Short skirts also gave the strongest impression of sexual interest, showing how much people can read into a hemline.

Long skirts fell between short skirts and blouses on confidence, while ordinary trousers scored higher than tracksuit bottoms on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Onesies gave the strongest impression of happiness and scored about as high as short skirts for confidence.

White clothes suggested a happier wearer than grey clothes did, with black clothes coming last.

These examples show how the impression changes with the question being asked: a blouse came out ahead for intelligence, while a onesie came out ahead for happiness.

The researchers began by asking about 200 people what they thought clothes could tell them about someone and comparing their answers with traits examined in previous research.

They then gathered ratings on 5,000 photographs from online shops, covering five kinds of impressions: intelligence, confidence, trustworthiness, happiness and sexual interest.

Participants formed these impressions from photographs of the garments alone, without seeing anyone wearing them.

The results showed that who was doing the judging explained more of the variation in ratings than which garment they saw.

For example, one person might associate tracksuit bottoms with training for a race, while another might picture someone spending a Sunday on the sofa.

The researchers draw a parallel between judging people by their clothes and judging them by their faces:

“That is, much like inferences from faces, the inferred attributes often lie in the eye of the beholder.”

The study was published in the Journal of Computational Social Science (Rosenbusch et al., 2021).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9581. Add This Packet Of Seasoning To Pot Roast For A Delicious Southern-Style Sandwich

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Pot roast is one of those simple homemade meals that may take a long time to cook but is pretty hands-off in the Crock Pot. Just brown the meat, add your ingredients, and let the cooker do its job. There are plenty of ways to upgrade a basic pot roast and some interesting regional pot roast dishes, and this simple trick is a bit of both. To give your pot roast a hint of Southern twang, add a packet of dry ranch seasoning. Similar to a set-it-and-forget-it easy French dip sandwich but Southern, a bit of ranch in your pot roast will give you some delightfully intense flavor and get you darn near a classic Mississippi pot roast.

Ranch seasoning is basically an off-the-shelf, ready-to-go spice packet containing multiple seasonings — usually salt, onion powder, garlic powder, and other dried herbs and spices, like parsley and black pepper. Most brands also contain buttermilk and whey, which will add a bit of a creaminess factor, but you don't have to worry about the roast tasting like a bottle of ranch dressing because the mix will cook down with added beef stock and natural juices to form a nice, thick gravy. It will come out rich, bold, and savory with just a hint of tanginess from the buttermilk. Once your roast is nice and tender, you can simply slice it (or shred it) up and serve it Italian-beef or French-dip style, preferably with some melted cheese on top. The first bite through the bread into the perfectly tender and umami-rich, seasoned beef will make you a believer.

If you want to go for a more or less standard pot roast route, you can simply rub your roast with a packet of Hidden Valley Ranch Seasoning, available online and in stores, or something similar, and cook it how you normally would with beef stock, potatoes, onions, carrots, and whatever other veg you like to use. To go full-on Mississippi roast, you can forgo the veggies and slow cook it with the ranch coating, beef stock or au jus gravy mix, and a half dozen or more whole pepperoncini. Up the spice level with extra hot peppers or use the whole jar. You can even add a bit of the brine for some supplementary heat, plus a zingy kick of vinegar. This will get you closer to an actual Mississippi pot roast, which typically features said peppers.

For the bread, something that will hold up to the moisture of the roast is ideal. Toasted French bread adds a crunchy texture, but a toasted hoagie roll works great, and a thick sourdough will add a little extra tang. You'll want a cheese that melts easily, so you can quickly broil it without overcooking the bread. A simple mozzarella is an easy, mild choice, but a nice Gruyère will bring a richer and nuttier flavor with some subtle sweetness.

Ranch-seasoned pot roast or the full Mississippi mix is also great on egg noodles, mashed potatoes, or rice, or you can make a simple open-faced sando with a thick Texas toast. For an even saltier, more savory roast, you can try a three-packet blend with ranch, brown gravy, and Italian-style salad dressing mixes. However, to get that good Southern flavor, don't veer too far off the ranch.
